title: Indigenous Traditions of Africa, the Americas and the Pacific
bigQuestion: How do traditions without one written book pass on what they hold sacred, and how have they survived being pushed aside?

story.title: The Ceremony Comes Back Outside
story.kicker: A ceremony that was against the rules in 1900 is held in the open a century later.
paragraphs: It is a summer morning in the year 2000 on a reservation in the northern Plains. Families park their trucks at the edge of a wide field. Children carry folding chairs. An elder walks slowly to the center, where people have built a circle for a ceremony. Singers gather around a large drum. Nobody is hiding. A local newspaper has even printed the date.

The elder is in her eighties. She remembers her grandmother's stories about a very different time. Around 1900, U.S. government rules banned many Native American ceremonies. Agents on reservations could punish people for dancing or for holding religious gatherings. Some families kept the ceremonies alive in secret, far from the agency buildings. Others lost them.

Her grandmother was also sent away to a boarding school. There, teachers cut her hair and punished her for speaking her own language. She was taught that her family's prayers were wrong. When she came home years later, she had to learn her traditions again from the old people who still remembered.

Now the drum begins. The elder listens to the songs her grandmother once sang in a whisper. In 1978, Congress passed a law saying that the United States would protect Native American religious freedom. Laws alone do not bring a tradition back. People do that, by teaching, remembering and gathering. Today, this ceremony is held in the open.
story.think: What would a community need to do to keep a ceremony alive if it could not be written down or practiced in public?

lessons.title: Scripture Without a Book
lessons.mainIdea: In many Indigenous traditions, sacred teachings are passed on by voice, song and ceremony instead of a written book.
reading: On a winter night in a Great Lakes community, an Ojibwe elder begins a story. Children sit close. In many Ojibwe families, some sacred stories are told only in winter, when snow covers the ground. The elder does not read from a page. She speaks the story as it was told to her, and as it was told to her own grandmother.

Scholars call this *oral tradition*. It means teachings, stories, songs and history passed from person to person by speaking and listening. In many Indigenous traditions, oral tradition does the work that a written scripture does in other religions. It holds the teachings a people treat as sacred. It explains how the world began and how people should live.

Oral tradition is not careless or loose. Many communities train certain people to remember long stories, songs and prayers exactly. Some use objects to help memory, such as Ojibwe birchbark scrolls with drawn figures, or beaded belts among some Eastern nations. The *elder*, a respected older person who carries knowledge, often decides when and how a teaching is shared.

words.d: teachings, stories and history passed on by speaking and listening rather than by writing
a respected older member of a community who carries and teaches its knowledge
describing the first peoples of a land and their descendants

look.title: A Book and a Voice
look.text: In one room, a student reads a sacred book. She can open it on any day and read any page. In another room, a child listens to an elder tell a sacred story. It is told only in winter, only by certain people, and it is never written down.
look.prompt: Name one thing each way of passing on teachings does well. Why might a community choose to keep a story oral?

check.q: What does oral tradition mean?
choices: Teachings passed on by speaking and listening
A sacred book kept in a temple
Prayers read silently from a page
check.why: Oral tradition is knowledge passed from person to person by voice, not by writing.

check.q: In many Ojibwe families, when are some sacred stories told?
choices: Only in winter, when snow is on the ground
check.why: The reading says many Ojibwe families tell some sacred stories only in winter.

check.q: Which object helps some Ojibwe people remember teachings?
check.why: Birchbark scrolls with drawn figures help some Ojibwe people remember sacred teachings.

lessons.title: Ancestors, Land and Seasons
lessons.mainIdea: Many Indigenous traditions tie the sacred to ancestors, to a specific homeland and to the turning seasons.
reading: In autumn, Ojibwe families in Minnesota and Wisconsin paddle canoes into shallow lakes to gather wild rice. They call it *manoomin*. One person pushes the canoe with a long pole. Another bends the stalks and taps the grain into the boat. Many Ojibwe people describe wild rice as a sacred gift. Their oral tradition says their ancestors traveled west to the place where food grows on the water.

This harvest shows three ideas found in many Indigenous traditions. The first is the land. Many traditions teach that a people belongs to a particular place, with its rivers, hills and animals. The second is the *ancestors*, family members who lived long ago. Many communities honor them and believe they stay connected to the living. The third is the seasons. Ceremonies often follow planting, harvest, hunting or the return of the sun.

These ideas differ from nation to nation. Still, many adherents describe the relationship with land as a duty, not ownership. The land gives food and medicine. People give thanks, take only what they need and care for it for those not yet born.

words.d: family members who lived long ago; in many traditions they are honored and remembered
the Ojibwe word for wild rice, a food many Ojibwe people treat as a sacred gift

look.title: Thanks Before the Harvest
look.text: Before a harvest, some families offer tobacco or a prayer of thanks. They take the rice, fish or plants they need and leave the rest. They say the next generation must find the land as healthy as they did.
look.prompt: What does this practice show about how these families see the land? Use the word ancestors or seasons in your answer.

check.q: What is manoomin?
choices: The Ojibwe word for wild rice
check.why: Manoomin is the Ojibwe word for wild rice, which many Ojibwe people see as a sacred gift.

check.q: According to the reading, how do many adherents describe their relationship to the land?
choices: As a duty of care, not ownership
As the same in every nation
check.why: Many adherents describe the land as a relationship of duty and care, not simple ownership.

check.q: Why do many Indigenous ceremonies happen at certain times of year?
choices: Because they follow the seasons, like planting and harvest
Because a king set the dates
check.why: Many ceremonies follow the seasons, such as planting, harvest and hunting.

lessons.title: Olodumare and the Orisha
lessons.mainIdea: Yoruba tradition teaches of a supreme being, Olodumare, and many orisha who each guide part of life and nature.
reading: Each August in the city of Osogbo, in southwestern Nigeria, crowds walk to a sacred grove beside the Osun River. A young woman carries a covered calabash on her head, and drummers follow her. The festival honors Osun, whom adherents associate with the river, with fresh water, healing and children. The grove is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Osun is one of the *orisha*. In Yoruba tradition, the orisha are powerful spirit beings who each watch over part of nature and human life. Ogun is linked with iron and work. Sango is linked with thunder and justice. Yemoja is linked with the waters and with mothers. Above them, Yoruba tradition teaches of *Olodumare*, the supreme being, who is far above daily life.

The Yoruba are one of the largest peoples of West Africa, living mostly in Nigeria and Benin. Today many Yoruba people are Muslim or Christian. Others follow the orisha tradition, and some people combine practices. Worship of the orisha includes songs, drumming, offerings and festivals. Each town and family may have its own special orisha.

words.d: in Yoruba tradition, spirit beings who each watch over part of nature and human life
in Yoruba tradition, the supreme being, above the orisha

look.title: Matching the Orisha
look.text: A student makes a chart. Osun: rivers, fresh water, healing. Ogun: iron, tools, work. Sango: thunder, justice. Yemoja: the waters, mothers. A blacksmith, a family by a river, and a judge each look at the chart.
look.prompt: Which orisha might each person feel closest to, according to the chart? What does this show about how the tradition connects to daily life?

check.q: In Yoruba tradition, who is Olodumare?
choices: The supreme being, above the orisha
A priest who reads palm nuts
check.why: Yoruba tradition teaches that Olodumare is the supreme being, far above daily life.

check.q: Which orisha do adherents link with iron and work?
check.why: In Yoruba tradition, Ogun is linked with iron, tools and work.

check.q: Which statement about Yoruba people today is accurate?
choices: All Yoruba follow only the orisha
Yoruba people live mainly in Japan
Many are Muslim or Christian, and others follow the orisha
check.why: Today many Yoruba people are Muslim or Christian, while others follow the orisha tradition.

lessons.title: Ifa: Reading for Guidance
lessons.mainIdea: In Ifa divination, a trained priest recites memorized verses to help a person seek guidance.
reading: A woman sits on a mat across from a *babalawo*, a trained Ifa priest. She has a hard choice to make. The priest casts a chain of seed pods onto a mat, or marks signs in powder on a round wooden tray. The pattern points to one of many sacred signs. Then he begins to recite verses tied to that sign.

This practice is called *divination*, a way of seeking guidance about a choice or a problem. In Yoruba tradition, Ifa divination is linked to Orunmila, the orisha of wisdom. The system has 256 signs, called odu. Each odu has many verses full of stories, advice and examples. A babalawo trains for many years to learn them by heart.

The verses are a large body of oral literature. The priest does not simply tell the future. He shares stories that fit the person's question, and the person thinks about what they mean. In 2005, UNESCO recognized the Ifa divination system as an important part of the world's cultural heritage.

words.d: a practice of seeking guidance or hidden knowledge about a question or problem
a trained priest of Ifa in Yoruba tradition
the 256 signs of Ifa, each with many memorized verses

look.title: A Library in Memory
look.text: Ifa has 256 signs. Each sign has many verses. A babalawo memorizes them over many years. He recites the right verses when a person brings a question.
look.prompt: How is Ifa like a written scripture, and how is it different? Give one example of each.

check.q: What is a babalawo?
check.why: A babalawo is a trained Ifa priest in Yoruba tradition.

check.q: How many signs, or odu, does the Ifa system have?
check.why: The Ifa system has 256 signs called odu, each with many verses.

check.q: Which orisha is Ifa divination linked to?
check.why: In Yoruba tradition, Ifa is linked to Orunmila, the orisha of wisdom.

lessons.title: Traditions Formed Under Slavery
lessons.mainIdea: Enslaved Africans carried their traditions to the Americas, where they grew into Santeria, Candomble and Vodou.
reading: In a home in Havana, Cuba, a small altar holds a statue of a Catholic saint. Beside it sit stones, shells and bowls. To a visitor, it may look like a Catholic shrine. To a follower of Santeria, the saint also calls to mind an orisha. This pairing grew during slavery, when many enslaved people could not practice their African traditions openly.

From the 1500s to the 1800s, the transatlantic slave trade forced millions of Africans across the ocean. Many were Yoruba, Fon or from Kongo peoples. They carried their songs, prayers and spirits in memory. In Cuba, Yoruba traditions grew into *Santeria*, also called Regla de Ocha or Lucumi. In Brazil, they grew into *Candomble*. In Haiti, Fon, Kongo and Catholic elements joined in *Vodou*.

These are sometimes called diaspora traditions. A *diaspora* is a people scattered far from their homeland. Many adherents see the saint and orisha pairing as a way their ancestors protected their faith. Today, these traditions have temples and followers in the Americas, including in U.S. cities such as Miami, New York and Chicago.

words.d: a people scattered far from their homeland, and the communities they form
a Cuban tradition rooted in Yoruba worship of the orisha, also called Regla de Ocha or Lucumi
a Brazilian tradition rooted in West African religions, including Yoruba worship of the orisha
a Haitian tradition joining West and Central African religions with Catholic elements

look.title: One Altar, Two Meanings
look.text: On a home altar in Cuba stands a statue of Saint Barbara in a red robe. A Catholic neighbor sees a saint. A follower of Santeria sees the saint and also thinks of Chango, the orisha of thunder, whose color is red. Under slavery, such pairings let people keep praying in their own way.
look.prompt: Why might a pairing like this have helped enslaved people keep their faith? What does it show about how traditions change in a new land?

check.q: In which country did Santeria take shape?
check.why: Santeria, also called Regla de Ocha or Lucumi, took shape in Cuba.

check.q: What does diaspora mean?
choices: A people scattered far from their homeland
check.why: A diaspora is a people scattered far from their homeland.

check.q: Why did many adherents pair orisha with Catholic saints, according to the reading?
choices: Because the Bible told them to
To protect their faith when they could not practice openly
Because the orisha came from Europe
check.why: Many adherents see the pairing as a way ancestors protected their faith under slavery.

lessons.title: Many Nations, Many Traditions
lessons.mainIdea: There is no single Native American religion; each nation has its own language, stories and ceremonies.
reading: A Hopi village in Arizona, a Lakota community in South Dakota and a Tlingit town in Alaska are all Native American. Yet their languages, stories and ceremonies are very different. The Hopi calendar follows farming in the desert. Tlingit ceremonies honor clan ancestors along the coast. Lakota ceremonies grew up on the open Plains.

The United States recognizes more than 570 tribal nations. Each is a *sovereign nation*, meaning it has its own government. Each also has its own traditions. So it is not accurate to speak of one Native American religion. Scholars and Native people often say traditions or ways of life instead. Many Native languages have no separate word for religion, because the sacred runs through all of life.

Many Native people today also practice Christianity, and some combine Christian and traditional ways. The Native American Church uses peyote, a small cactus, as a sacrament in prayer meetings. Its members come from many nations. This variety is one reason students should name the specific nation when they describe a practice.

words.d: a people with its own government; U.S. law recognizes tribal nations this way
a religious movement drawing members from many nations, which uses peyote as a sacrament

look.title: Say Which Nation
look.text: Sentence A: Native Americans hold a ceremony for the summer sun. Sentence B: Many Lakota communities hold a summer ceremony that is sacred to them.
look.prompt: Which sentence is more accurate, and why? What mistake does Sentence A make about Native traditions?

check.q: About how many tribal nations does the United States recognize?
check.why: The United States recognizes more than 570 tribal nations, each with its own traditions.

check.q: Why is it not accurate to speak of one Native American religion?
choices: Because Native people have no ceremonies
Because each nation has its own language, stories and ceremonies
Because all nations follow the Hopi calendar
check.why: Each nation has its own traditions, so there are many Native traditions, not one.

check.q: What does the Native American Church use as a sacrament?
check.why: The Native American Church uses peyote, a small cactus, as a sacrament in prayer meetings.

lessons.title: Nations of the Great Lakes
lessons.mainIdea: The Potawatomi, Ojibwe and Miami peoples lived in the Great Lakes region, including the land that is now Chicago.
reading: Walk along the Chicago River today and you are on land where the Potawatomi once lived and traded. Many historians say the name Chicago comes from a Miami-Illinois word, shikaakwa, for a wild onion that grew along the river. The Potawatomi, Ojibwe and Odawa call themselves the Anishinaabe. They have long described themselves as the Council of Three Fires.

Many Anishinaabe families teach the *Seven Grandfather Teachings*. They are wisdom, love, respect, bravery, honesty, humility and truth. Each teaching is often linked to an animal. The Ojibwe also have the Midewiwin, a society that keeps healing knowledge and sacred teachings. The Miami people, whose homeland included parts of Indiana and Illinois, have their own language and ceremonies.

In the Treaty of Chicago of 1833, the Potawatomi gave up their last lands in the area. By the late 1830s, most were forced west. The Miami were forced out of Indiana in 1846. Today, Potawatomi nations live in Kansas, Wisconsin, Michigan and elsewhere. The Miami Tribe of Oklahoma works to bring back the Myaamia language. Chicago has one of the largest urban Native communities in the country.

words.d: the name shared by the Ojibwe, Odawa and Potawatomi peoples and related nations
Anishinaabe teachings of wisdom, love, respect, bravery, honesty, humility and truth
an Ojibwe society that keeps healing knowledge and sacred teachings

look.prompt: How many years passed between the Treaty of Chicago and the removal of the Miami from Indiana?

check.q: Which three peoples make up the Council of Three Fires?
check.why: The Ojibwe, Odawa and Potawatomi describe themselves as the Council of Three Fires.

check.q: Which is one of the Seven Grandfather Teachings?
check.why: Humility is one of the seven, along with wisdom, love, respect, bravery, honesty and truth.

check.q: What happened after the Treaty of Chicago of 1833?
choices: The Potawatomi built the Bahá'í temple

check.why: After the 1833 treaty, most Potawatomi were forced to move west by the late 1830s.

lessons.title: Banned, Then Protected
lessons.mainIdea: U.S. policy once banned many Native ceremonies and sent children to boarding schools; the 1978 law declared a duty to protect Native religious freedom.
reading: In 1883, the U.S. government issued rules called the Code of Indian Offenses. They made many Native ceremonies, such as the Sun Dance, punishable on reservations. Agents could withhold food rations or jail people who took part. Some communities kept ceremonies going in secret. Many sacred objects were taken and sent to museums.

At the same time, the government and many churches ran *boarding schools* for Native children. The Carlisle Indian Industrial School in Pennsylvania opened in 1879. Children were taken far from home, given new names and punished for speaking their languages. Many never came home. The schools aimed at *assimilation*, making people give up their own culture for the majority's.

Native people pushed back for decades. In 1978, Congress passed the *American Indian Religious Freedom Act*. It said the United States would protect Native people's right to practice their traditional religions, visit sacred sites and use sacred objects. In 1994, Congress added protection for the use of peyote by members of the Native American Church.

words.d: a school where students live; U.S. Indian boarding schools separated Native children from their families and cultures
pressure on a group to give up its own culture and take on the majority culture
a 1978 U.S. law stating the policy of protecting Native American religious practice

look.title: The 1978 Law
look.text: The United States will protect and preserve the right of American Indians, Eskimos, Aleuts and Native Hawaiians to believe, express and practice their traditional religions. This includes access to sacred sites, use and possession of sacred objects, and freedom to worship through ceremonies and traditional rites.
look.cite: American Indian Religious Freedom Act, Public Law 95-341, 1978, Section 1 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Name two things this law says it will protect. Why might each matter to a Native community?

check.q: What did the Code of Indian Offenses of 1883 do?
choices: Made many Native ceremonies punishable on reservations
check.why: The 1883 Code of Indian Offenses made many ceremonies, like the Sun Dance, punishable.

check.q: What does assimilation mean?
choices: Pressure to give up one's culture for the majority's
check.why: Assimilation is pressure to give up one's own culture and take on the majority's, the goal of the boarding schools.

check.q: What year did Congress pass the American Indian Religious Freedom Act?
check.why: The American Indian Religious Freedom Act was passed in 1978; peyote protection was added in 1994.

lessons.title: Tapu, Mana and the Sea
lessons.mainIdea: Many Polynesian traditions teach of mana, a sacred power, and tapu, rules that set sacred things apart.
reading: At a Maori marae in New Zealand, a group of visitors waits at the edge of an open courtyard. A woman from the home community calls out to them in a chant. The visitors walk forward slowly. Speeches and songs follow. At the end, hosts and guests press noses and foreheads together in the hongi. Only then are the visitors treated as part of the gathering.

The welcome follows ideas found across Polynesia. *Mana* is a sacred power or authority that people, places and objects can hold. *Tapu* means set apart, sacred or restricted. A tapu person or place must be approached with care and the right rules. In Hawaiian the word is kapu. The English word taboo comes from this Polynesian word.

Polynesian peoples crossed thousands of miles of ocean in voyaging canoes, finding their way by stars, waves and birds. Many trace their family lines back to ancestors and to the gods. The Maori call this *whakapapa*, or genealogy. Knowing one's whakapapa tells a person who they are and where they belong.

words.d: in Polynesian traditions, set apart as sacred or restricted; the source of the English word taboo
in Polynesian traditions, sacred power or authority held by people, places or objects
the Maori word for genealogy, linking a person to ancestors, land and the gods

lessons.title: Revival and Respect Today
lessons.mainIdea: Indigenous communities are reviving languages and ceremonies, and outsiders show respect by following each community's protocol.
reading: In the 1970s, a group of Hawaiians built a voyaging canoe called Hokule'a. In 1976 it sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti with no modern instruments, guided by stars and swells. The voyage helped spark a Hawaiian renaissance. Hula schools, the Hawaiian language and old chants grew strong again. Across North America and Africa, communities are doing similar work.

Revival also brings questions about respect. Many ceremonies are private. Some songs belong to certain families or clans. Some knowledge is shared only with people who have trained for it. This is called *protocol*, the proper way of doing something according to a community's rules. Visitors may be asked not to take photos, or to wait to be invited.

In 2007, the United Nations adopted the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. It says Indigenous peoples have the right to practice their spiritual traditions and to protect sacred sites. For a student, respect means learning what a community has chosen to share, naming the nation, and not copying sacred items as costumes or crafts.

words.d: the proper way of doing something according to a community's rules
bringing a language, practice or tradition back into common use

look.title: A Global Promise
look.text: Indigenous peoples have the right to practice, develop and teach their spiritual and religious traditions, customs and ceremonies. They have the right to keep up, protect and privately reach their religious and cultural sites, and to use and control their ceremonial objects.
look.cite: United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, 2007, Article 12 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: How is this promise like the 1978 U.S. law? What does it add by covering Indigenous peoples in every country?

check.q: What was the Hokule'a?
choices: A Hawaiian voyaging canoe that sailed to Tahiti in 1976
check.why: Hokule'a is a Hawaiian canoe that sailed to Tahiti in 1976 by stars and swells.

check.q: What is protocol?

check.why: Protocol is the proper way of doing something according to a community's rules.

check.q: Which is a respectful way for a student to study an Indigenous tradition?

check.why: Respect means learning what is shared, naming the nation and following protocol.
